translation.text:
…to establish them in the faith.

Therefore[f], believe God—you who, on account of your sins, have despaired of your life, and are adding sin to sin, and are burdening your life—that if you turn back to the Lord with your whole heart and work righteousness for the remaining days of your life, and serve him rightly according to his will, he will make healing for your former transgressions[b], and you will have power to gain mastery over the works of the devil. And do not at all fear the devil’s threat; for he is strengthless, like the sinews of a dead man[c].

Listen to me, then, and fear the One who is able to do all things, to save and to destroy[d]; and keep these commandments, and you will live to God.

I say to him, “Lord, now I have been strengthened in all the righteous requirements of the Lord, because you are with me; and I know that you will cut off all the devil’s power, and we shall gain mastery over him and prevail against all his works. And I hope, Lord, that now I can keep these commandments that you have commanded, with the Lord strengthening me.”

“You will keep them,” he says, “if the turning is toward your own city[a].

Foolish, double‑minded, and wretched man, do you not understand that all these things are alien, and are under the authority of another? For the lord of this city will say, ‘I do not want you to dwell in my city; rather, go out from this city, because you do not make use of my laws.’ So then, you—having fields and dwellings and many other possessions—when you are cast out by him, what will you do with your field and your house, and the rest of the things you have prepared for yourself? For the lord of this land says to you, rightly, ‘Either make use of my laws, or withdraw from my land.’ So then, what are you about to do, having…[e]

footnotes.text: The Greek reads irregularly, “if the turning (ἡ κάμψαι) is to your own city.” Many editors suspect a scribal lapse (e.g., τό for ἡ, or an omitted μή). The parable that follows supports the sense of orienting toward one’s true city.
Greek ἴασιν can mean healing or cure. Some translations smooth to “forgiveness/remission,” but Hermas’s moral-therapeutic imagery is likely intentional.
In antiquity sinews were a metaphor for strength. Saying the devil is like the sinews of a dead man underscores utter powerlessness.
This phrasing echoes early Christian speech about God as the one able to save and to destroy (cf. echoes in James 4:12; Matt 10:28), though Hermas is not directly quoting.
The Greek text in this source slice breaks off mid-sentence here (“So then, what are you about to do, having…”); the unit continues in the next segment.
Or 'believe in God—you who, on account of your sins, have despaired of your life, and are adding sin to sin, and are burdening your life—for if you turn back'.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render as “turn back to the Lord with your whole heart.”
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas emphasizes moral reorientation and ongoing obedience, not only cognitive change or a technical conversion term. ‘Turn back’ reflects volition and relational return.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: “He will make healing for your former transgressions.”
alternative_readings: He will forgive your former sins
He will grant remission of your past sins
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas’s moral-struggle discourse frequently uses therapeutic metaphors for sin; preserving ‘healing’ maintains that texture without denying the judicial aspect implied by ‘transgressions.’

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Translate διάβολος as “devil,” preserve the vivid image of impotence “like the sinews of a dead man.”
theological_decisions.rationale: In Hermas, διάβολος functions as the personal adversary. The image underscores the contrast between God’s power and the devil’s threats, fitting the paraenetic aim.

theological_decisions.issue: Dative of reference in “you will live to God”
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Retain the literal idiom “live to God.”
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas’s register often mirrors early Christian idiom; rendering the dative preserves that feel and leaves interpretive space for readers.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render both occurrences as “Lord,” leaving the referential tension in place (“Lord” addressed, and “with the Lord strengthening me”).
alternative_readings: Differentiate as ‘master’ for the speaker and ‘Lord’ for God
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas’s visions often blur angelic agency and divine commission; preserving the lexical sameness reflects that ancient texture rather than resolving it for modern readers.

theological_decisions.issue: Conditional clause on turning to one’s own city
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: “You will keep them … if the turning is toward your own city.”
alternative_readings: if you do not turn aside to your own city
if you turn aside to your own city
theological_decisions.rationale: The transmitted Greek is irregular; the ensuing parable clarifies the sense: one must orient toward one’s true city (God’s realm) rather than invest in the foreign city (this world). The chosen rendering keeps the metaphor’s direction without over-fixing the Greek.

source.text: τοῦ Θεοῦ. 9. εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ ἐπλούτισεν ὑμᾶς ὁ δεσπότης, ἵνα ταύτας τὰς διακονίας τελέσητε αὐτῷ· πολὺ βέλτιόν ἐστι τοιούτους ἀγροὺς ἀγοράζειν [καὶ κτήματα] καὶ οἴκους, οὓς εὑρήσεις ἐν τῇ πόλει σου, ὅταν ἐπιδημήσῃς εἰς αὐτήν. 10. αὕτη ἡ πολυτέλεια καλὴ καὶ ἱλαρά, λύπην μὴ ἔχουσα μηδὲ φόβον, ἔχουσα δὲ χαράν. τὴν οὖν πολυτέλειαν τῶν ἐθνῶν μὴ πράσσετε· ἀσύμφορον γάρ ἐστιν ὑμῖν τοῖς δούλοις τοῦ Θεοῦ· 11. τὴν δὲ ἰδίαν πολυτέλειαν πράσσετε, ἐν ᾗ δύνασ δίδωσιν, ἐρριμμένη δὲ χαμαὶ σαπρὸν καὶ ὀλίγον φέρει. αὕτη οὖν ἡ παραβολὴ εἰς τοὺς δούλους τοῦ Θεοῦ κεῖται, εἰς πτωχὸν καὶ πλούσιον. 5. Πῶς, φημί, κύριε; γνώρισόν μοι. Ἄκουε, φησίν· ὁ μὲν πλούσιος ἔχει χρήματα πολλά, τὰ δὲ πρὸς τὸν Κύριον πτωχεύει περισπώμενος περὶ τὸν πλοῦτον αὐτοῦ, καὶ λίαν μικρὰν ἔχει τὴν ἐξομολόγησιν καὶ τὴν ἔντευξιν πρὸς τὸν Κύριον, καὶ ἣν ἔχει, μικρὰν καὶ βληχρὰν καὶ ἄνω μὴ ἔχουσαν δύναμιν. ὅταν οὖν ἀναβῇ ὁ πλούσιος ἐπὶ τὸν πένητα καὶ χορηγήσῃ αὐτῷ τὰ δέοντα, πιστεύων ὅτι ὃ ἐργάσεται εἰς τὸν πένητα δυνήσεται τὸν μισθὸν εὑρεῖν παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ—ὅτι ὁ πένης πλούσιός ἐστιν ἐν τῇ ἐντεύξει [καὶ τῇ ἐξομολογήσει,] καὶ δύναμιν μεγάλην ἔχει ἡ ἔντευξις αὐτοῦ παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ— ἐπιχορηγεῖ οὖν ὁ πλούσιος τῷ πένητι πάντα ἀδιστάκτως· 6. ὁ πένης δὲ ἐπιχορηγούμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ πλουσίου ἐντυγχάνει αὐτῷ, τῷ Θεῷ εὐχαριστῶν περὶ τοῦ διδόντος αὐτῷ. κἀκεῖνος ἔτι ἐπισπουδάζει περὶ τοῦ πένητος, ἵνα ἀδιάλειπτος γένηται ἐν τῇ ζωῇ αὐτοῦ· οἶδε γὰρ ὅτι ἡ ἔντευξις τοῦ πένητος προσδεκτή ἐστι καὶ πλουσία πρὸς τὸν Θεόν. 7. ἀμφότεροι οὖν τὸ ἔργον τελοῦσιν· ὁ μὲν πένης ἐργάζεται τὴν ἔντευξιν ἐν ᾗ πλουτεῖ, [ἣν ἔλαβεν ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου·] ταύτην ἀποδίδωσι τῷ Κυρίῳ τῷ ἐπιχορηγοῦντι αὐτῷ. καὶ ὁ πλούσιος ὡσαύτως τὸν πλοῦτον ὃν ἔλαβεν ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου ἀδιστάκτως παρέχει τῷ πένητι. καὶ τοῦτο ἔργον μέγα ἐστὶ καὶ δεκτὸν παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ, ὅτι συνῆκεν ἐπὶ τῷ πλούτῳ αὐτοῦ καὶ εἰργάσατο εἰς τὸν πένητα ἐκ τῶν δωρημάτων τοῦ Κυρίου καὶ ἐτέλεσε τὴν διακονίαν τοῦ Κυρίου ὀρθῶς. 8. παρὰ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις οὖν ἡ πτελέα δοκεῖ καρπὸν μὴ φέρειν, καὶ οὐκ οἴδασιν οὐδὲ νοοῦσιν ὅτι, ἐὰν ἀβροχία γένηται, ἡ πτελέα ὕδωρ ἔχουσα τρέφει τὴν ἄμπελον, καὶ ἡ ἄμπελος ἀδιάλειπτον ἔχουσα ὕδωρ διπλοῦν τὸν καρπὸν δίδωσι, καὶ ὑπὲρ ἑαυτῆς καὶ ὑπὲρ τῆς πτελέας. οὕτω καὶ οἱ πένητες ἐντυγχάνοντες πρὸς τὸν Κύριον ὑπὲρ τῶν πλουσίων

translation.text:
For to this end the Master has made you rich[1], that you might carry out these ministries for him; it is far better to buy such fields [and estates] and houses, which you will find in your city when you arrive in it. This luxury is good and cheerful, having no grief nor fear, but having joy. So do not practice the luxury of the nations; for it is unprofitable for you, the servants of God. Rather practice your own luxury, in which you are able to rejoice. For all luxury of this kind is profitable. But the luxury of the nations is bitter and harsh. This parable, then, is set before the servants of God, for the poor and the rich.

‘How so, sir?’ I say. ‘Make it known to me.’ ‘Listen,’ he says: ‘The rich man has much money, but toward the Lord he is poor, being distracted about his wealth, and he has very little confession and intercession toward the Lord; and what he has is small and feeble, and has no power to go up above. When, therefore, the rich man goes to the needy and supplies him with what is necessary, believing that what he does for the needy he will be able to find as his wage from God—for the needy is rich in intercession [and in confession], and his intercession has great power with God—the rich man supplies the needy with everything without doubting. And the needy, being supplied by the rich, intercedes for him, giving thanks to God on behalf of the one who gives to him. And that one is still more eager concerning the needy, so that he may be unceasing in his life; for he knows that the intercession of the needy is acceptable and abundant with God. Therefore both complete the work: the needy performs the intercession in which he is rich, [which he received from the Lord;] this he renders to the Lord for the one who supplies him. And likewise the rich man without doubting provides to the needy the wealth which he received from the Lord. And this is a great work and acceptable with God, because he understood concerning his wealth and worked for the needy out of the gifts of the Lord and fulfilled the Lord’s ministry rightly. Therefore, among people the elm seems not to bear fruit; and they do not know nor understand that[2], if there should be a drought, the elm, having water, nourishes the vine, and the vine, having unceasing water, gives double fruit, both for itself and for the elm. In the same way also the needy[b][a][14][13][12][11][10][9][8][7][6][5][4][3], interceding with the Lord on behalf of the rich...

footnotes.text: "and estates" (καὶ κτήματα) appears bracketed in the Greek; some witnesses include it, others omit it.
ἐπιδημήσῃς can mean "be present as a resident/visitor"; here, the thought is of arriving again at one’s own city, an eschatological image in Hermas.
Hermas pointedly redefines "luxury" as joyful, fear-free generosity that stores up for life in the coming city.
The Greek δοῦλοι τοῦ Θεοῦ is rendered "slaves of God" to preserve the ownership-and-obedience nuance; "servants" is a smoother but less exact alternative.
"and in confession" (καὶ τῇ ἐξομολογήσει) is bracketed; the phrase may be a scribal addition or gloss.
ἔντευξις is a specific term for petitionary approach/intercession; alternatives are "petition" or general "prayer."
The clause likely means the needy person is sustained continually by the rich man’s care. Some take it of the rich man’s own constancy in doing good.

For to this end the Master has made you rich, that you might carry out these ministries for him; it is far better to buy such fields [and estates][1] and houses, which you will find in your city when you arrive in it[2]. This luxury is good and cheerful[3], having no grief nor fear, but having joy. So do not practice the luxury of the nations[14]; for it is unprofitable for you, the slaves of God[4]. Rather practice your own luxury, in which you are able... it gives; but when it is thrown to the ground it bears rotten and little fruit.[11] This parable is set for the slaves of God, for the poor and the rich.

‘How so, sir?’ I say. ‘Make it known to me.’ ‘Listen,’ he says: ‘The rich man has much money, but toward the Lord he is poor, being distracted about his wealth, and he has very little confession and intercession[6] toward the Lord; and what he has is small and feeble, and has no power to go up above. When, therefore, the rich man goes up to the needy and supplies him with what is necessary, believing that what he does for the needy he will be able to find as his wage[13] from God—for the needy is rich in intercession [and in confession][5], and his intercession has great power with God—the rich man supplies the needy with everything without doubting. And the needy, being supplied by the rich, intercedes for him, giving thanks to God on behalf of the one who gives to him. And that one is still more eager on behalf of the needy, so that he may be unceasing in his life[7]; for he knows that the intercession of the needy is acceptable and abundant with God[8]. Therefore both complete the work: the needy performs the intercession in which he is rich [which he received from the Lord][12]; this he renders to the Lord for the one who supplies him. And likewise the rich man without doubting provides to the needy the wealth which he received from the Lord. And this is a great work and acceptable with God, because he came to understand about his wealth and worked for the needy out of the gifts of the Lord and fulfilled the Lord’s ministry rightly[9]. Therefore, among people the elm[10] seems not to bear fruit; and they do not know nor understand that, if there should be a drought, the elm, having water, nourishes the vine, and the vine, having unceasing water, gives double the fruit, both for itself and for the elm. In the same way also the needy, interceding to the Lord on behalf of the rich...’

translation.text: Therefore, believe God—you who, on account of your sins, have despaired of your life, and are adding sins and weighing down your life—that if you turn back to the Lord with your whole heart and work righteousness for the remaining days of your life, and serve him rightly according to his will, he will bring healing to your former sins, and you will have power to gain mastery over the works of the devil. And do not at all fear the devil’s threat; for he is powerless, like the sinews of a dead man.

translation.text:
“How is that so, sir?” I ask. “Explain it to me.”

“Listen,” he says. “A rich man has plenty of money, but he is poor in what concerns the Lord. His wealth distracts him, so he offers very little confession before God or prayer for others. What he does offer is weak and has no power to rise to God.

“But when the rich man helps a needy person and provides what he needs, he believes that God will reward him for it. The needy person is rich in prayer for others and in confession before God,[a] and his prayer has great power with God. So the rich man provides everything the needy person requires, without hesitation. In return, the needy person prays for him and thanks God for the one who helped him. Then the rich man becomes even more eager to care for the needy person, so that the needy person can continue living, because he knows that the needy person’s prayer is rich and acceptable before God.

“In this way, together they complete the work. The needy person offers the prayer in which he is rich—something he received from the Lord—and presents it to the Lord for the person who supports him. Likewise, the rich man freely shares with the needy person the wealth he received from the Lord. This is a great work that pleases God, because the rich man understood how he should use his wealth. He used the Lord’s gifts to help the needy and faithfully carried out the Lord’s service.

“To people, the elm appears to bear no fruit. But they do not know or understand that during a drought, when the elm has water, it nourishes the vine. Because the vine has a constant supply of water, it produces twice the fruit—fruit for itself and for the elm. In the same way, when needy people pray to the Lord for the rich...”
